proof:
# Equal-area endpoints and their exact Minkowski midpoint: a planar depth bound

Let A,B be arbitrary planar convex bodies of the same positive area a. Put

    M=(A+B)/2, m=|M|, y=g_M,
    C=conv(({−1} x A) union ({1} x B)),
    S=C intersect (Z x R^2).

Then C is an actual three-dimensional convex body, its ONLY integer fibers are A,M,B at -1,0,1, and the point (0,y) belongs to S. Every closed ambient halfspace H containing (0,y) satisfies

    vol_MI(S intersect H) >= kappa vol_MI(S),

where

    kappa=4(22+12sqrt(2))/[9(57+12sqrt(2))]
          =0.234150579... >2/9.                                    (1)

Thus the planar n=1 OC bound holds in this exact-midpoint, equal-end-area class. The statement does NOT replace M by an arbitrary convex superbody, does not identify g_M with the average of the endpoint centroids, and is not an arbitrary-dimensional OC theorem. The stricter constant in (1) is a proved lower bound, not claimed sharp.

The mechanism combines two independent paired-tail estimates. A proposed sharper linear-volume payment fails even at g_M, as proved separately in `candidate af4e7610828e864b`; that false inequality is not used here.

## 1. A width-based paired-tail bound in every dimension

First let d>=1, let A,B have equal positive d-volume a, and put M=(A+B)/2 and y=g_M. For u!=0 set w_A=h_A(u)+h_A(-u)>0 and define w_B,w_M similarly. Then w_M=(w_A+w_B)/2. The elementary centroid support estimate gives

    h_M(u)-u.y>=w_M/(d+1).                                           (2)

To prove it, normalize the u-projection of M to [0,1], choose a point at its minimum, and note that the homothet with ratio s about that point is contained in {u.x<=s}. The projection CDF is therefore at least s^d. Integrating its complement bounds the projected centroid by d/(d+1), proving (2).

For arbitrary t, let the two cap heights below the maximal supports be

    delta_A=h_A(u)-(u.y+t), delta_B=h_B(u)-(u.y-t).

Their sum is at least (w_A+w_B)/(d+1). Hence at least one ratio delta_A/w_A, delta_B/w_B is at least 1/(d+1). An actual homothety of that body about a supporting maximal point, with scale 1/(d+1), is contained in the corresponding captured halfspace. Consequently

    |A intersect {u.x>=u.y+t}|+|B intersect {u.x>=u.y-t}|
                       >=a/(d+1)^d.                                (3)

This covers negative heights, supporting thresholds and full caps: the argument only uses the body whose ratio is positive, and a ratio above one captures that whole body.

For d>=2, Hölder gives the stronger direction-specific form

    paired mass >=
      a (w_A+w_B)^d /
        [(d+1)^d (w_A^(d/(d-1))+w_B^(d/(d-1)))^(d-1)].               (4)

If either height reaches the whole width, its full captured volume a already exceeds this right side (the dimensionless ratio is at most 2/(d+1)^d<=1). Otherwise replace negative height ratios by zero; their width-weighted sum remains at least (w_A+w_B)/(d+1). Apply Hölder to this weighted sum and the d-th powers of the two nonnegative ratios, then use the actual cap homotheties. Thus (4) does not assume the two cuts are proper.

For clarity, width ratios can themselves be bounded by the actual Minkowski volume, without assuming that a width-realizing segment is parallel to u. Choose p,q in A with u.(q-p)=w_A, and put v=q-p. The set B+[p,q] lies in A+B and has volume

    a+||v|| vol_(d-1)(proj_(v perpendicular) B).

Every line section of B parallel to v has length at most w_B||v||/w_A. Fubini therefore gives

    vol_(d-1)(proj_(v perpendicular) B)>=a w_A/(w_B||v||),
    2^d m>=a(1+w_A/w_B).                                            (5)

The reversed statement gives the reciprocal bound. This oblique Fubini justification is needed; an arbitrary width-realizing segment need not give a simple comparison with projection onto u perpendicular. Formula (5) is supplementary below; the proof of (1) needs only (3).

## 2. An independent residual Brunn--Minkowski bound

Let Gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d and r=m/a>=1. For every same pair of halfspaces centered at g_M,

    paired mass >=a [1-{2[(1-Gamma_d)r]^(1/d)-1}^d]_+.              (6)

Here is the complete argument. Write U,V for its captured volumes. If U+V>=a, the inequality is immediate. Otherwise set q=a-U-V>0. The complementary closed truncated bodies have volumes a-U,a-V. Their midpoint is contained in the residual halfspace {u.x<=u.g_M} of M. By ordinary Grünbaum at g_M, that halfspace has volume at most (1-Gamma_d)m. Brunn--Minkowski yields

    (a-U)^(1/d)+(a-V)^(1/d)<=2[(1-Gamma_d)m]^(1/d).

For two numbers in [0,a] with sum a+q, concavity of the 1/d power makes their root sum at least a^(1/d)+q^(1/d). Rearrangement proves (6). All complementary boundary sections are null for full-dimensional convex bodies, so the use of closed halfspaces changes no volume. Positive residual volumes hold in the only nontrivial case U+V<a.

In d=2, (3) and (6) therefore give the simultaneous uniform bound

    paired mass/a >= max{1/9,F(r)},
    F(r)=4sqrt(5r)/3-20r/9.                                         (7)

The positive-part notation from (6) can be omitted in this maximum because 1/9 is positive.

## 3. Every ambient halfspace at the actual middle centroid

Move a containing halfspace parallel until its boundary passes through (0,y); this only decreases its measure. A nonvertical such halfspace has the form

    u.x+alpha z>=u.y, u!=0.

Its endpoint thresholds are u.y+alpha on A and u.y-alpha on B, precisely the pair controlled in (7). The own middle cap contributes at least (4/9)m by ordinary Grünbaum. Since total mixed area is 2a+m, every such halfspace has normalized mass at least

    G(r)=[(4/9)r+max{1/9,F(r)}]/(r+2).                              (8)

For a purely integer normal, the closed through-source halfspace contains all of M and at least one endpoint fiber, giving mass m+a and normalized value (r+1)/(r+2)>=2/3. This is larger than (1). Thus no oblique or purely integer normal is omitted, and all boundary masses of the latter case are retained.

A short direct check already gives the OC constant. On 1<=r<=3/2,

    F(r)-(4/9)(1-r/2)=[12sqrt(5r)-18r-4]/9>0.

The numerator is concave, so its minimum on that interval occurs at an endpoint. At r=1 it is 12sqrt(5)-22>0, as 720>484; at r=3/2 it is 12sqrt(15/2)-31>0, as 1080>961. For r>=3/2, 1/9>=(4/9)(1-r/2). Adding the own (4/9)r contribution proves the normalized 2/9 bound directly. This calculation makes the exact scope of the positive argument transparent.

## 4. The uniform margin in (1)

For r>=1 the function F is strictly decreasing. Its unique crossing with 1/9 is

    r_*=(17+12sqrt(2))/20.

Indeed F(r)=1/9 is equivalent to 12sqrt(5r)=20r+1, whose squared equation is 400r^2-680r+1=0; only the displayed root belongs to [1,infinity). On [1,r_*], (8) equals

    [12sqrt(5r)-16r]/[9(r+2)].

Its derivative has the sign of 6sqrt(5)(2-r)/sqrt(r)-32, which is strictly negative for r>=1 (for r<=2, bound (2-r)/sqrt(r)<=1; for r>=2 it is nonpositive). On [r_*,infinity), (8) equals

    (4r+1)/[9(r+2)],

whose derivative is positive. Therefore its global minimum is at r_*, with value

    (4r_*+1)/[9(r_*+2)]
       =4(22+12sqrt(2))/[9(57+12sqrt(2))]=kappa.

Finally kappa-2/9=2(12sqrt(2)-13)/[9(57+12sqrt(2))]>0. This proves the exact uniform margin and completes the theorem.
